hook.line: Altamira's offer is generous, and everybody knows it. Tomás still wants to say no. To admit a fact and carry on anyway, Spanish reaches for *aunque*.
hook.es: Aunque Altamira paga bien, no nos vamos.
hook.en: Even though Altamira pays well, we're not leaving.

examples.es: Aunque es tarde, hay mucha gente en el café.
examples.en: Even though it's late, there are lots of people in the café.

examples.es: Aunque no me gusta, lo hago.
examples.en: Even though I don't like it, I do it.
We're going to walk even though it's raining.

examples.es: Aunque el apartamento es pequeño, tiene una vista maravillosa.
examples.en: Even though the flat is small, it has a wonderful view.

examples.es: Hernando camina mucho, aunque tiene setenta años.
examples.en: Hernando walks a lot, even though he's seventy.

examples.es: Aunque estudié mucho, no pasé el examen.
examples.en: Although I studied a lot, I didn't pass the exam.
Are you working today even though it's Sunday?

rule:
*Aunque* means even though or although. It brings in a fact that should have stopped something, and then that something happens anyway.

It rains, and we walk anyway: *Vamos a caminar aunque llueve.*

The verb after *aunque* is the normal one you already know: *es*, *llueve*, *tengo*, *estudié*. You're stating a real fact.

*Aunque* can open the sentence (put a comma after the first part) or sit in the middle, just like English.

Compare it with *porque*: *porque* gives the reason something happens, *aunque* gives the reason it shouldn't have. And *Aunque es caro, lo compro* says the same as *Es caro, pero lo compro*. Use one or the other, never both.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a concessive clause. Later you'll meet *aunque* with a different verb form for even if, about things that aren't settled yet.

options: We go out because it's raining.
We go out even though it's raining.
We don't go out because it's raining.
We don't go out because it's raining.
We go out even though it's raining.
I'm buying it even though it's cheap.
I'm buying it because it's cheap.
It's expensive, so I'm not buying it.
I'm buying it because it's expensive.
It's expensive, but I'm buying it.

readAndPick.es: Aunque tengo hambre, no quiero comer.
options: I'm hungry, but I don't want to eat.
I'm not hungry, so I don't want to eat.
We work because it's Sunday.
We don't work on Sundays.
We work even though it's Sunday.

readAndPick.es: Aunque Rosa ya no está, el café sigue abierto.
options: Rosa is gone, so the café is closed.
Rosa is gone, but the café is still open.

readAndPick.es: Aunque no hablo bien, entiendo mucho.
options: I don't speak well, but I understand a lot.
I speak well, so I understand a lot.
I don't understand much because I don't speak well.

readAndPick.es: Aunque hace frío, Tomás abre la ventana.
options: Tomás opens the window because it's cold.
Tomás opens the window even though it's cold.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *aunque* or *porque* and type the whole sentence: *Vamos a caminar ___ llueve.* (We're going to walk even though it's raining.)
yourTurn.why: The rain should stop the walk and doesn't: *aunque*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *aunque* or *porque* and type the whole sentence: *Lo compro ___ es barato.* (I'm buying it because it's cheap.)
yourTurn.why: Cheap is the reason you buy it, so *porque*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Even though it's Sunday, we're working.
yourTurn.why: *Aunque* plus a plain fact, then what happens anyway.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Even though I'm tired, I'm going to work. (going to your job)
yourTurn.answer: Aunque estoy cansado, voy al trabajo.
accept: Aunque estoy cansada, voy al trabajo.
Voy al trabajo aunque estoy cansado.
Voy al trabajo aunque estoy cansada.
yourTurn.why: Being tired is the fact you admit; it doesn't stop you.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Hernando walks a lot, even though he's seventy.
yourTurn.answer: Hernando camina mucho, aunque tiene setenta años.
accept: Aunque tiene setenta años, Hernando camina mucho.
yourTurn.why: Age in Spanish is *tener*, and *aunque* can sit in the middle like even though.

yourTurn.prompt: Rewrite with *aunque* instead of *pero*: *Es caro, pero lo compro.*
yourTurn.why: *Aunque* moves to the fact you admit, and *pero* disappears.

yourTurn.prompt: Rewrite with *aunque*: *No tengo mucha plata, pero voy a hacer el viaje.*
yourTurn.answer: Aunque no tengo mucha plata, voy a hacer el viaje.
accept: Voy a hacer el viaje aunque no tengo mucha plata.
Aunque no tengo mucho dinero, voy a hacer el viaje.
yourTurn.why: Same meaning, one connector: *aunque* in front of the obstacle.

pitfalls.wrong: Aunque es caro, pero lo compro.
pitfalls.why: Almost. In English you'd never say although it's expensive, but I buy it; Spanish doesn't either. One connector is enough.
Rain isn't why you walk; it's what you walk in spite of, so *aunque*.
The day of the week takes *es*, with or without *aunque* in front.

personal: What do you do even though it isn't easy? Write two true sentences with *aunque*: one starting with it, and one with it in the middle.
